card.hook: Here's a nice problem to have: a gate, a very long brick wall, the Cathedral and the Giralda all crowd into one view, and you get a whole open square to back up in.
card.stand_here: Stand in the centre of Plaza del Triunfo and face the Puerta del León, the Alcázar's main gate. Step back until the whole entrance and the brick walls fit on your screen.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the gate and walls in one frame. If the square is busy and you can't step back any further, switch to zoom 0.5x. Then try zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for details of the gate and the brickwork.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sunlit wall, then slide the brightness down a little (darker) so the brick keeps its colour and the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning. That's when guides say the facade catches direct sun.
card.selfie_here: Try Calle Agua in Barrio Santa Cruz: the palace wall runs along one side of the lane, and in spring and summer bougainvillea hangs overhead. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the palace wall over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Just past the ticket check, ask someone to stand back across the courtyard and photograph you in front of the carved, tiled facade of the Palace of Pedro I, so it fills the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Guides disagree on selfie sticks, and the palace itself may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official Alcázar site before you go.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines and see if you can get the gate dead centre with the walls perfectly level. Bonus points if nobody's head sneaks in.
card.good_to_know: The site began as an Islamic-era citadel in the 10th century. The best-known part today is the richly decorated Mudéjar palace Pedro I built in the 1360s. It's still one of the official residences of the Spanish royal family, and it was made a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, together with the Cathedral and the General Archive of the Indies.

card.hook: Picture a giant half-circle of brick and tile curving around a canal, with a tower at each end. Now picture seeing the whole thing from a balcony, which is the shot everyone wants.
card.stand_here: Take one of the staircases along the building up to the upper gallery balconies above the arcades, near the central section of Plaza de España. Face out over the balustrade so the canal, the central fountain and both towers all fit in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze in the whole curve, the canal and both towers. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look at the central section. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the towers, the tilework and the alcoves.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the facade, then slide a little darker so the sky and the brick both keep their detail.
card.best_time: Early morning gives you the emptiest frames, but the sun reportedly rises behind the main building, so much of the plaza stays in shade until late morning. Crowds build from about 10-11 AM, and the central bridges get busy then.
card.selfie_here: Stand on one of the four canal bridges, turn side-on and use the front camera so a tower sits behind you. For a close, colourful backdrop, sit on the tiled bench in one of the provincial alcoves with the blue-and-white tiles behind you.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone by the Vicente Traver fountain in the heart of the square, and stand in front of the fountain so both towers rise on either side of you.
card.rules_and_safety: Entry has been free, but access is reported to be changing in 2026 and an entrance fee has been discussed, so check the official site before you go. The canal is sometimes drained, so be ready to shoot the architecture instead.
card.challenge: Find the alcove for your home province, or the one with the prettiest tiles, and get a photo of yourself sitting in it.
card.good_to_know: Plaza de España was built in 1928 for the Ibero-American Exposition of 1929 and designed by Aníbal González. The four bridges over the canal each stand for one of the ancient kingdoms of Spain, and the tiled alcoves each represent a province. You might also recognise it from Star Wars: Episode II - Attack of the Clones.

card.hook: In 1401 the cathedral chapter reportedly decided to build a church so grand that people would take them for mad. Stand in front of it and you'll see they pulled it off.
card.stand_here: Stand in the far south-eastern corner of Plaza del Triunfo and face north-west. From here the cathedral is to the north-west, about 2 minutes on foot, so walk towards the walls and the Giralda tower you can see from far off.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole south side with the Giralda above it. If the square is busy or you want more building in, tap 0.5x. Try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the top of the Giralda and the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stonework, then drag the slider to make the picture a little darker so the sky doesn't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early, ideally before about 9am. The square is nearly empty and the south front is nicely lit.
card.selfie_here: Try the edge of the La Terraza del EME rooftop (Calle Alemanes 27). Use the front camera and tap 0.5x if you can, because the Giralda is only about 30 m away and can sit right behind you. It's a hotel rooftop bar, so you may need to be a customer.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the right side of Plaza del Triunfo (as you face the cathedral) and step back across the plaza, while you stand in front of the facade, because the building is too big to fit in one frame up close.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos inside the cathedral are allowed without flash. The outside views from the squares are free, but entry to the cathedral and the Giralda may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site first.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, line the Giralda up with a vertical line, and see if you can make the tower stand perfectly straight.
card.good_to_know: Seville Cathedral is the largest Gothic cathedral in the world, built on the site of a great 12th-century mosque, the Almohad mosque. The Gothic building alone is 126 m long and 76 m wide, and the Giralda reaches 104.5 m to its weather vane. Work finished in 1506-7, and Christopher Columbus is buried inside.

card.hook: Picture a forest of giant wooden mushrooms growing out of a city square, with you standing right underneath. Locals call it Las Setas, "the Mushrooms", and the name fits.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the sweep of the parasols overhead. Switch to 1x for tidier, less stretched shots, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for close-ups of the timber grid.

card.best_time: Early or late in the day should give the wood a warmer colour. If it's lit after dark, try night mode and hold your phone steady against a rail or your body.

card.rules_and_safety: Personal photography is generally allowed, but commercial photography or drones may need special permits, so check the signs on site. The rooftop walkway narrows near the bends, so step to one side when you stop for photos.
card.challenge: Take one shot looking straight up for a perfectly symmetrical pattern, then one a little lower with a few strangers in it, so the mushrooms look as big as they are.
card.good_to_know: Metropol Parasol was designed by German architect Jürgen Mayer and finished in April 2011. It's roughly 150 by 70 metres and about 26 metres high, made of six parasols inspired by the vaults of Seville Cathedral and the ficus trees in Plaza de Cristo de Burgos. Underneath are a market and a small museum of Roman and Moorish remains. The rooftop terrace and museum may be ticketed or have set hours, so check the official site before you go.

card.challenge: Take one shot where the gateway's curves frame your head like a fancy marble hat, then check whether you can still see the sky behind it.
card.good_to_know: Casa de Pilatos is still the permanent home of the Dukes of Medinaceli, and building began in 1483. The marble gateway was designed in 1529. Inside, around 150 different tile designs from the 1530s make up one of the largest early tile collections in the world.

card.hook: Dark ironwork, pale walls, orange trees all around: Plaza de Santa Cruz is a tiny stage set that happens to be real. Even better, you can have it to yourself if you beat the tour groups.
card.stand_here: Step onto the paths in the raised central garden of Plaza de Santa Cruz, right beside the wrought-iron Cruz de la Cerrajería. Aim at the cross so the hedges and orange trees fill the sides of your picture.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the cross and its garden. Go to 0.5x for the whole square, but keep the cross away from the edges so it doesn't stretch. Then try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) for the ironwork and orange-tree details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the cross on a vertical line. Then tap the cross and slide it a touch darker so the white walls and bright sky keep their detail.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, before the tour groups arrive, and it's much quieter. Soft light early or late in the afternoon is kinder than harsh midday sun.
card.selfie_here: Head to Calle Agua (Callejón del Agua), the narrow lane along the old Alcázar wall. Stand under the bougainvillea that hangs over the street in spring and summer, use the front camera, and let the whitewashed alley sit behind you. For a bigger backdrop, stand in the orange-tree square of Patio de Banderas, reached through the arched passage next to the Alcázar, so the Giralda rises behind you.
card.ask_someone: On Calle Mateos Gago, ask a passer-by to stand across the street from the front of the Iglesia de Santa Cruz so the whole facade and you both fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Casual photos are generally fine in public lanes and squares, but check the rules at the entrance of museums, patios and religious sites, as they can differ. The square looks like open public space, but check the official sites before you go for nearby ticketed sights like the Cathedral or Real Alcázar.
card.challenge: Take the cross at 1x, then walk closer and catch just one orange branch curling into the corner. Pick your favourite and call it 'Cross, with Citrus'.
card.good_to_know: Santa Cruz is the old Jewish quarter of Seville. Ferdinand III of Castile gathered the city's Jewish community here after he took Seville. The square is named after a Mudéjar church that was pulled down during the Napoleonic Wars, and the painter Murillo was buried in it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Step onto the paths in the raised central garden of Plaza de Santa Cruz, right beside the wrought-iron Cruz de la Cerrajería. Aim at the cross so the hedges and orange trees fill the sides of your picture.

card.hook: Picture a row of orange trees leading to an archway, with a 50-metre tower filling the gap like a painting that's already framed. That's the Giralda from Patio de Banderas, and the frame comes free.
card.stand_here: Walk into Patio de Banderas (you reach it from the Alcázar exit), where the Giralda is to the north-west, about 3 minutes on foot. Stand at the far end by the exit archway and look back toward the cathedral side.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the tower fills the archway. Try zoom 0.5x if you'd like more of the orange trees and the square, or zoom 2x to get closer to the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on your gridlines so the tower stays upright and the arch sits level.
card.best_time: Early morning is calmest, and the low sun lights the tower through the arch. You'll have more room to wander, too.
card.selfie_here: Try Calle Mateos Gago, the tree-lined street near the tower. Use the front camera, zoom 0.5x, and stand in the street with the Giralda over your shoulder, trees framing it. Patio de los Naranjos, the orange-tree courtyard inside the cathedral complex, is another backdrop with the tower rising beside you.
card.ask_someone: At Plaza Virgen de los Reyes, ask a passer-by to stand across the square, ideally on the right-hand side when facing the cathedral, while you stand in front of the tower so the whole Giralda fits in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the cathedral, photos are fine but flash isn't allowed. The cathedral and tower may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the tower dead centre in the archway with the orange trees leading straight to it, then see if a friend can spot which tree you used as your guide.
card.good_to_know: The Giralda began as a minaret, commissioned in 1171 for the city's great mosque and finished on 10 March 1198, when four metal spheres were set on top. Inside, 35 ramps wind up the core instead of stairs. The cathedral and the Giralda have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987, along with the Alcázar and the General Archive of the Indies.

card.hook: Here's a tower that gets to show off twice: once standing on the riverbank, and again upside down in the Guadalquivir. The best view is from the other side of the water.

card.good_to_know: The Torre del Oro is a twelve-sided tower built around 1220-21 to help control boat traffic on the river. It was once one of two anchor points for a great chain stretched across the water. The name means 'Tower of Gold', linked to the golden shine of its building materials. The slim round top level was added in 1760, after the 1755 Lisbon earthquake damaged the original top, and the people of Seville objected when there was a plan to knock the tower down.

card.hook: A king on horseback, a long calm town hall behind him and a big open floor to back up on: Plaza Nueva is about as tidy a photo as Seville hands out.
card.stand_here: Stand on the open floor of Plaza Nueva, facing the Ayuntamiento (town hall). The statue of Ferdinand III is about 40 m to the west, so turn until the statue sits in front of you with the long facade spread out behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the statue and the facade together. Tap 0.5x if you want the whole square and more sky, or 2x (or higher, depending on your phone) for the horse and rider up close.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the statue on one of the vertical lines and keep the facade running level across the frame.
card.best_time: Soft light early or late in the day tends to flatter pale buildings. If you're there after dark, use night mode and hold your phone steady against your body or a firm ledge.
card.selfie_here: Stand by the equestrian statue of King San Fernando in the middle of the square, with the town hall's neoclassical facade behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and let the statue and facade sit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the corner where Calle Méndez Núñez meets the square and shoot across the plaza, so the town hall facade and open square fill the frame with you by the statue.
card.rules_and_safety: Leave the selfie stick at home: it's banned in most paid places in Seville, though that's not stated for the open square itself. Pickpockets work in crowds, so keep your bag on you rather than hanging it on a chair.
card.challenge: Crouch a little and see if you can make the horse and rider stand out against the building instead of the sky. Bonus points if the facade stays perfectly level.
card.good_to_know: The statue shows Ferdinand III, who took Seville for the Christians in 1248 and was later declared a saint, and it was inaugurated in August 1924. The town hall facade dates from the 18th century. The square itself is young, finished in 1856 on land that belonged to a big convent from 1270 until 1840, and only the little San Onofre chapel survives.

card.hook: Here's a fun surprise: the church looks like it's been here forever, but it was only finished in 1949. Put it next to a chunk of Seville's old city wall and you get old stone and a twentieth-century church in one picture.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza de la Esperanza Macarena, in front of the basilica entrance, then walk toward the main road and turn right. Face the old city wall running along the road, with the old government building across the road behind it. The map pin may not match the plaza exactly, so check where you are on the ground.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the wall and the building across the road. Tap 0.5x if you've got room and want more wall in the frame. At the arch, try zoom 2x or 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the basilica's spire.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the top edge of the wall with a horizontal line so it sits level.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the wall and the gate than midday. That's a general rule of thumb, so check the light when you get there.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Arco de la Macarena, the city gate beside the basilica, and stand on the pedestrianised area in front of the arch. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it), hold it a little low and put the gate over your shoulder, with the basilica just beside it.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot straight through the archway of the Arco de la Macarena so the church spire shows on the far side, and check the framing on the spot because there's no set place to stand.
card.rules_and_safety: The square and the wall are public, but the basilica is a place of worship with its own opening times, so check the official site before you go. Keep flash off near the altar and during services.
card.challenge: Traffic and passers-by are part of the scene, so take a few frames of the wall and pick the cleanest one, then see if you can get the spire peeking through the arch.
card.good_to_know: The basilica was founded in 1941, designed by Sevillan architect Aurelio Gómez Millán and finished in 1949. It became a minor basilica in 1966, and a museum about Seville's Holy Week opened here in 2009. It's home to the Virgin of Hope of Macarena and the Jesús de la Sentencia sculptures.

card.hook: From the street, the Hospital de la Caridad looks calm and polite. Step inside and it's all baroque gold and carving, which is a fun switch to catch on your phone.
card.stand_here: Follow the phone icon on the map to the hospital, close to Seville's Real Maestranza bullring. For the outside shot, step back into the street in front of the hospital and face the façade, so the whole building fits in one frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the doorway and façade. If the street is too narrow to fit it all in, try 0.5x, but keep your phone level so the walls don't lean. Inside, zoom 2x is handy for carvings and gilded details.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines and line the walls up with the vertical lines, then tap a mid-tone part of the wall and slide darker if bright windows or sky are washing out.
card.best_time: Outside, an overcast sky or soft morning or late-afternoon light keeps the façade nice and even. Inside, go when the chapel is open and quiet.
card.selfie_here: Go into the main courtyard and head for the corner straight ahead after the main gate. Use the front camera, and if your phone has it, try 0.5x so the yellow walls and blue-and-white tiles frame you with the hospital over your shoulder. Then wander over to the Dutch ceramic panels and fountains for a second one.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Calle Temprado, outside the main entrance at number 3, facing the baroque front gates and bell tower, while you pose in front of the gates.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working charity hospital and a place of worship, so dress respectfully, be discreet around residents and services, and check the official site for visiting and photo rules. Photos are generally allowed inside, but reflections on the paintings can spoil shots, so move around until the glare disappears.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole façade with dead-straight walls, then one close-up of a single detail, and see which one you like more.
card.good_to_know: The Hospital de la Caridad was founded in 1674 and still cares for older and frail people. Its chapel is described as holding some of the city's richest baroque sculpture. Murillo painted eight works for the brotherhood he belonged to in 1668: four stayed in Seville, and the other four were taken in 1810 and now hang in galleries abroad.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Follow the phone icon on the map to the hospital, close to Seville's Real Maestranza bullring. For the outside shot, step back into the street in front of the hospital and face the façade, so the whole building fits in one frame.

card.hook: This place was once the second largest building in Spain, so your main job here is simply squeezing it into your phone. Good news: it's calm, tidy and very patient.
card.stand_here: Stand on Calle San Fernando, on the far side of the street from the main entrance (the Puerta de la Fama). Face the building so the arched entrance sits right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the straight-on view. If the whole width won't fit from the pavement, tap 0.5x and keep the building away from the edges so the lines don't stretch. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the arch and the stone sculpture above it.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the entrance arch up with the centre line so both halves of the façade match.
card.best_time: There's no set time. Pick a moment when the façade is lit rather than in shadow, and tap the stone to see if the sky is washing out. If it is, slide it a little darker.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the entrance arch on Calle San Fernando with the arch and its stone carvings behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tuck the arch over your shoulder. If you can get into the Fountain Patio (it's inside the university, so access may be limited), the arcaded walls make a lovely backdrop too.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the far side of Calle San Fernando while you stand in front of the building, so the whole main façade fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Non-flash photos are fine in the public areas of the factory, and commercial photography needs prior permission. Keep to the pavement, don't step into the dry ditch, and watch for cars when you cross the street.
card.challenge: The carvings on the entrance arch show Columbus and Cortés, so see if you can get them in your selfie.
card.good_to_know: Building began in 1728, and from 1758 until the 1950s the factory made snuff and cigars. At its peak in the 1880s about 6,000 women worked here, and Bizet's fictional Carmen is a cigarrera from this factory. Today it houses the rectorate of the University of Seville, so the outside is what you're here for.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Calle San Fernando, on the far side of the street from the main entrance (the Puerta de la Fama). Face the building so the arched entrance sits right in front of you.

card.hook: Picture a whole building showing up twice in one photo: once the right way up, once upside down in the water. That's the trick of Plaza de América on a calm day.
card.stand_here: Walk to the central pond in the middle of the plaza inside the Parque de María Luisa. The phone icon marks the plaza itself, so head from it to the pond and face the Museum of Popular Arts and Traditions across the water.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the pond and the museum facade together. Go to 0.5x if you want the whole plaza, or 2x to pick out the tilework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the water's edge on a lower line, so the reflection fills the bottom third and the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is lovely, when the light warms the tiles. Early morning is quieter, so fewer people end up in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Stand beside the central fountain and its flower beds, where the water catches the sun in the daytime. For a livelier one, hold out a handful of birdseed among the doves and let them swirl around you. Use the front camera at 0.5x so a building fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand a few paces back at the central pond, facing the Museum of Popular Arts and Traditions, while you stand at the water's edge with the museum behind you across the pond.
card.rules_and_safety: There's little shade in the plaza unless you go back into the park, so watch the sun. Building work in the plaza may block some views, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one photo of each of the three buildings and see if your friends can match them to their styles: Neomudéjar, Neo-Renaissance and Gothic.
card.good_to_know: The architect Aníbal González designed the plaza for the Ibero-American exhibition of 1929, along with the three buildings around it. Those are the Museum of Popular Arts (Neomudéjar), the Archaeological Museum (Neo-Renaissance) and the Royal Pavilion (Gothic). The plaza has also been a film location, including for an episode of The Crown.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk to the central pond in the middle of the plaza inside the Parque de María Luisa. The phone icon marks the plaza itself, so head from it to the pond and face the Museum of Popular Arts and Traditions across the water.
